sections.title: Galaxies and their organization
sections.text:
A galaxy is a gravitationally associated system containing stars, interstellar gas, dust and a dark-matter component. A star is one luminous object; a galaxy can contain enormous numbers of stars. Our Solar System belongs to the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy. A constellation is a named pattern or region of the sky as seen from Earth, not necessarily a physically bound group of nearby stars.

Galaxy classification describes visible structure. Spiral galaxies have disks with spiral arms and central concentrations. Barred spirals have an elongated central bar. Elliptical galaxies range from nearly round to elongated forms and often contain older stellar populations. Irregular galaxies lack a simple regular shape. These categories describe morphology, not an inevitable progression through a fixed evolutionary ladder. Mergers, gas supply, star formation and gravitational interactions can change a galaxy over time.

Gas and dust form the interstellar medium. Cold molecular clouds can provide sites of star formation, while hot gas may trace energetic events. Dust absorbs and scatters light, sometimes hiding stars at visible wavelengths. Infrared observations can reveal regions that ordinary photographs miss. Observing at several wavelengths is therefore essential to understanding galaxy structure.

sections.title: How a star forms
sections.text:
Star formation begins when a sufficiently dense region of a gas cloud collapses under gravity. Collapse competes with pressure, turbulence and magnetic effects. As gas falls inward, gravitational energy becomes thermal energy. A central protostar develops, often surrounded by a rotating disk. Material may continue accreting while jets and radiation influence the surrounding cloud.

If the central temperature and pressure become high enough, sustained hydrogen fusion begins. The object enters the main sequence, the long-lived stage during which core hydrogen fusion supplies most of its energy. A star reaches an approximate balance between inward gravity and outward pressure. This hydrostatic balance does not mean every particle is stationary; matter and radiation continue transferring energy.

```text
Cold gas cloud → gravitational collapse → protostar and disk
→ sufficiently hot core → sustained hydrogen fusion → main-sequence star
```

The mass with which a star forms strongly affects its luminosity and lifetime. Massive stars contain more fuel but use it much faster, so they generally live shorter lives than low-mass stars. Stars shine through nuclear reactions and energy transport, rather than chemical burning in atmospheric oxygen.

sections.title: Fusion, energy transport and the Sun
sections.text:
Hydrogen fusion converts light nuclei into helium through reaction sequences. The final products have slightly less total rest mass than the initial reactants; the difference appears as energy according to $E=\Delta mc^2$. Here $E$ is energy in joules, $\Delta m$ is the corresponding mass difference in kilograms and $c$ is the vacuum speed of light in metres per second. The large value of $c^2$ explains why small mass differences can correspond to substantial energy.

The Sun's core produces energy primarily through the proton–proton chain. Radiation and convection transfer energy outward through different internal regions. The photosphere is the visible surface from which much observed sunlight emerges. Above it lie the chromosphere and corona. Magnetic fields produce phenomena including sunspots, flares and coronal mass ejections. Space-weather disturbances can affect satellites and technological systems near Earth. [NASA: Sun facts](https://science.nasa.gov/sun/facts/).

Fusion does not mean that the Sun will suddenly become a supernova. Its mass places it on a different evolutionary pathway from the most massive stars. Its future development must be understood in terms of changing fuel sources and internal structure.

sections.title: Brightness, temperature and spectra
sections.text:
Luminosity is the total power an object emits, measured in watts. Apparent brightness is the received power per unit area. For an unobscured source radiating uniformly,

$$F=\frac{L}{4\pi d^2},$$

where $F$ is flux in watts per square metre, $L$ is luminosity in watts and $d$ is distance in metres. Doubling distance reduces received flux to one quarter. Consequently, a faint-looking star may be intrinsically bright but distant.

Colour gives information about surface temperature: blue stars are generally hotter than red stars. A spectrum separates light into wavelengths. Absorption lines occur when atoms or ions absorb characteristic wavelengths, revealing composition and physical conditions. Doppler shifts can indicate motion along the line of sight. Spectroscopy therefore extracts information that a simple brightness measurement cannot provide.

The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram relates stellar luminosity to temperature or spectral type. Main-sequence stars form a broad band; giant stars are luminous because of their large radiating areas; white dwarfs can be hot yet faint because they are small. The diagram classifies physical states rather than plotting the stars' actual positions in space.

sections.title: Stellar endings and the origin of elements
sections.text:
When core hydrogen becomes depleted, a star's structure changes. A Sun-like star expands into a red giant and later sheds outer layers. Its exposed remnant becomes a white dwarf, supported by electron degeneracy pressure and gradually cooling. A planetary nebula is the expelled glowing material in this stage; despite the name, it is not the formation of planets.

Massive stars can undergo successive nuclear-burning stages and develop cores that can no longer remain supported. Core collapse can produce a supernova and leave a neutron star or black hole, depending on the star's history and remnant mass. A neutron star is extremely dense; a pulsar is a rotating neutron star whose emission beams are observed as pulses. A black hole has a boundary, the event horizon, from inside which outward-directed light cannot escape to distant observers.

Stellar fusion and explosive events enrich space with heavier elements. Later generations of stars and planets form from this enriched material. The carbon in organisms and many elements in Earth's rocks therefore connect biological and geological history to earlier stellar processes. Different elements have different production pathways; not all heavy elements are made by one kind of event.

**Mass, fuel and lifetime.** Stellar lifetime is governed by the ratio of usable nuclear fuel to the rate of energy release, not fuel quantity alone. A massive star's much greater luminosity can outweigh its larger fuel supply. Its core also follows a different pressure and temperature history. This is why a star's initial mass is central to predicting whether its final stages will resemble the Sun's pathway or involve core collapse. Binary interactions and mass loss can modify that history.

**Observing invisible remnants.** A black hole need not be seen as a luminous solid surface. Scientists can infer its presence from the motions of nearby matter, radiation from surrounding accreting gas and other evidence. Material outside an event horizon can emit strongly, while radiation emitted inside cannot escape to distant observers. A black hole does not attract a distant object more strongly than another object of the same mass at the same distance merely because it is a black hole.

**A worked brightness comparison.** Suppose two unobscured stars have equal luminosity but one is three times farther away. The inverse-square relation predicts that the more distant star supplies one ninth the received flux. If their apparent brightness is instead equal, the more distant star could have nine times the luminosity under the same assumptions. Extinction by intervening dust can change the comparison, showing why the physical assumptions belong with the calculation.

questions.prompt: What supplies the major long-term energy output of a stable main-sequence star such as the Sun?

options.D: Permanent reflection of light from distant galaxies

questions.explanation: Main-sequence stars release nuclear binding energy principally through hydrogen fusion.

questions.prompt: Two stars appear equally bright from Earth, but one is much farther away. Which conclusion is possible?

options.A: They must have the same intrinsic luminosity
options.B: The farther one must be colder
options.C: Their chemical compositions must be identical
options.D: The farther star may have a greater intrinsic luminosity

questions.explanation: Apparent brightness depends on intrinsic luminosity and distance. Equal observed brightness does not imply equal emitted power.

questions.prompt: A dark absorption line in a stellar spectrum can reveal information about:

options.A: Only the star's distance from Earth
options.B: Atomic or molecular species interacting with the light
options.C: The number of moons orbiting the star

questions.explanation: Atoms and ions absorb characteristic wavelengths associated with electronic transitions, enabling spectroscopy to infer composition and conditions.
